newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australians want to keep euthanasia law - poll.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australians want to keep euthanasia law - poll.

text.p: An overwhelming majority of Australians do not want their government to quash the world's first voluntary euthanasia law, in the outback Northern Territory, a poll published on Wednesday found.

The AGB-McNair poll, published in The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper ahead of parliamentary debate on the controversial law, found 75 percent of voters were against the national government overturning the territory's law.
Only 19 percent supported a private motion by government backbencher Kevin Andrews, who has the support of conservative Prime Minister John Howard, to revoke the measure.

The assisted suicide law took effect in the isolated territory from July, but prolonged legal and political wrangles delayed its use until two weeks ago, when a dying cancer sufferer in the territory capital, Darwin, became the first to suicide under the legislation.
Andrews, a leader of a strict-morals faction within the government, wants Howard's Liberal-National administration to use its constitutional powers to overturn the law.
Parliamentary debate on the Andrews motion is due to begin late this month. A vote is expected sometime this session, which is scheduled to end on December 5.
The latest poll -- the newspaper did not say how many people were questioned -- supports previous surveys showing about three in four Australians support assisted suicides.
Despite the poll's findings, the Herald supported the Andrews motion, saying in an editorial that sympathy for the Northern Territory parliament was misplaced.
"It is unimaginable that the larger, more mature State or Federal legislatures would pass such irresponsible laws," the paper said in an editorial.
"And it is just as well that the constitutional provision for over-riding such aberrations exists."

Under the constitution, the federal government has the power to overturn legislation passed by the two territory parliaments, but not laws adopted by legislators in Australia's six fully-fledged and more populous states.
The territory law allows dying patients to commit suicide by lethal injection or pills, subject to strict controls.
Leading pro-euthanasia campaigner doctor Philip Nitschke, who assisted in the first suicide, has said he has five more patients waiting to use the law.
